system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2127-02-08 18:07:00 to 2127-02-10 16:13:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and gastrostomy status was admitted after transfer for a clogged GJ tube. He had recently been treated for aspiration pneumonia with Unasyn and was weaned from mechanical ventilation and pressors prior to admission. The clogged feeding tube was successfully replaced via interventional radiology, allowing resumption of tube feeds and oral medications, including antiretroviral therapy. Mild transaminitis was noted with ultrasound showing gallstones but no cholecystitis; outpatient follow-up was recommended. He remained stable on trach collar with no respiratory deterioration. He was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing monitoring of liver enzymes and continuation of chronic medications.
problems: Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase and lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]
Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis without obstruction

EXAMINATION:  Chest x-ray

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with L PICC// CONFIRM PLACEMENT   Contact name:
___: ___

TECHNIQUE:  Portable chest x-ray

COMPARISON:  Previous x-ray from ___

FINDINGS: 

There is a left PICC with the tip in the region of the cavoatrial junction. 
There is a tracheostomy tube, similar in position to prior.  Low lung volumes
compromise evaluation.  There is persistent diffuse bilateral interstitial
opacities.  Allowing for differences in technique, this not significantly
changed.  There are no large pleural effusions.  Heart size appear similar.

IMPRESSION: 

Left PICC tip in region of kv O2 junction.  Heart and lungs appear similar to
the prior study from ___.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with malfunctioning GJ tube at OSH. Has foley in
place.// Please replace GJ tube

COMPARISON:  GJ tube exchange ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS:  Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology
Fellow and Dr. ___, attending radiologist performed the
procedure. Dr. ___ supervised the trainee during the key
components of the procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was used for local anesthesia
MEDICATIONS: None.
CONTRAST:  20 ml of Optiray
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  4.9 min, 27 mGy

PROCEDURE:  18 ___, 3.5 cm stoma length low profile gastrojejunostomy tube
exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
health care proxy. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and
placed supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per
___ protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile
fashion.

The existing Foley tube was injected with contrast and showed opacification of
the gastric rugae and duodenum.  A stiff glidewire was negotiated into the
stomach.  The balloon of the Foley was taken down and the catheter was removed
over the wire.  A 5 ___ Kumpe the catheter was advanced over the wire into
the stomach and negotiated into the jejunum with the Glidewire.  Position was
confirmed with contrast injection.  The Kumpe the was removed over the
Glidewire.  A new, 18 ___, 3.5 cm stoma length low profile
gastrojejunostomy tube was advanced over the wire into position under
fluoroscopy.  The balloon was inflated under fluoroscopic visualization. 
Contrast was administered through the jejunostomy and gastrostomy lumens to
confirm appropriate positioning.  The lumens were flushed and capped.  The
site was dressed.  The patient tolerated the procedure well without any
immediate complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Appropriately positioned new 18 ___ low profile gastrojejunostomy tube.

IMPRESSION:

stoma length low-profile MIC gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I know you were transferred because of your feeding tube issue. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’m okay. A little tired. I know my tube stopped working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that your GJ tube was displaced and may have caused some breathing issues and infection. Your vitals are stable now. We’ve placed a PICC line so we can give you antibiotics and nutrition safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I had pneumonia before. Is it back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did have signs of pneumonia when you came in—your chest X-ray showed more lung opacities. But it’s likely related to the tube being in the wrong place and some aspiration. You’ve already completed a course of penicillin for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube caused the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we think. When the tube moved out of position, it may have allowed stomach contents to go into your lungs. That’s why replacing it correctly is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Will I get a new tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Tomorrow morning, the interventional radiology team will replace your GJ tube. It’s a minimally invasive procedure, done with imaging guidance. You’ll be awake but comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local numbing medicine, so you might feel some pressure but not sharp pain. The team will walk you through each step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about my HIV meds? I need to keep taking them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Right now, you’re on IV nutrition and antibiotics. Once the new tube is in and we confirm it’s working, you’ll restart all your meds through the tube, including your HIV medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My sister usually helps me with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted she’s your contact. We’ll make sure she’s updated and knows how to manage the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for your tube replacement. The radiology team will do it in a few hours. Any questions before we go ahead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand. Just make sure it’s secure this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. They’ll use imaging to confirm it’s in the right spot—both in the stomach and the jejunum—before finishing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did great. The procedure was successful. You now have a new low-profile GJ tube. It’s in the right place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start slow with tube feeding and monitor you. Earlier, your blood sugar was a bit low, but it improved once we gave some IV nutrition. Now that the tube is working, we can keep your levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I get shaky if I go too long without feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re restarting feeds gradually. We’ll also flush the tube daily with sodium bicarbonate to help prevent clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do that at home. I use baking soda.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same thing. It helps keep the tube clear. We’ll make sure your care team at the extended facility knows your routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lung sounds are clearer today. The infection is resolving, and your oxygen levels are back to baseline. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Not as short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re still on oxygen through your trach, but no need for increased support. We’ll keep using glycopyrrolate and chlorhexidine rinses to reduce secretions and prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I use those at home. They help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue all your regular meds: Keppra for seizures, omeprazole for reflux, citalopram and lorazepam for anxiety. Everything will go through the new tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to miss any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made good progress. Your labs this morning are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Today? That’s fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because the main issue—the tube—was fixed, and you’re responding well. Your breathing is back to normal, and you’re tolerating feeds without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up for the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pneumonia was treated, and your lungs are improving. No specific follow-up is needed unless you develop fever or breathing trouble. Just keep up with your regular HIV and respiratory care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV? My last CD4 was 168, undetectable viral load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s stable. Keep taking your HAART regimen—Darunavir, ritonavir, and Truvada—as prescribed. Your care team will monitor your CD4 and viral load as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the tube—what if it clogs again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Flush it daily with water and baking soda, as you’ve been doing. If it ever stops draining or feeding, don’t force it—call your care team. They can assess it before it becomes an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions to your sister and the facility. You’ll be going home with the same meds and routine, just with a new, working tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be on your way by early afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Your tube site looks clean, no redness or drainage. You’re on full tube feeds and all meds are being given properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feels fine. No pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: keep up with the flushes, take your meds, and call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or tube issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad we could help get you back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and GJ tube dependence was admitted after transfer for a malfunctioning feeding tube that was displaced and likely caused aspiration pneumonia. He was stabilized, and a new GJ tube was successfully placed via interventional radiology. Nutrition was resumed, resolving mild hypoglycemia, and all chronic medications, including antiretrovirals, were restarted through the tube. His respiratory status improved to baseline, and he was discharged to extended care with instructions to maintain tube care and medication routines.
